newsitem.title: USA: Commodity firms weigh value of hedging programs. [CORRECTED 18:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Commodity firms weigh value of hedging programs. [CORRECTED 18:00 GMT]

text.p: For anyone wondering whether hedging boosts a commodity firm's bottom line, the answer is a resounding maybe.
At least that was the message conveyed by industry executives gathered at a conference here on Thursday.
Most commodity producers and end-users use hedging as a shield against unpredictable price fluctuations, though hedging strategies vary widely from one company or industry to another.

"I think (hedging) can add shareholder value, but it depends on the financial situation of the company," Joseph Simmons, general manager of supply and demand at Philadelphia-based Sun Co Inc, the independent U.S. oil refiner and marketer, told participants at a conference on commodities investing sponsored by Goldman, Sachs & Co.

Sun's three-year-old hedging program has helped the company to avoid financial distress, Simmons said. The second largest importer of crude oil in the U.S., Sun can be anywhere from five percent to 95 percent hedged on its crude purchases, Simmons said.
For companies whose core business depends on a steady supply of a particular commodity, a sharp rise in prices can wreak havoc with its balance sheet.
In 1991, the huge jump in jet fuel prices at the beginning of the Gulf War caught several airlines who weren't hedged off guard, and was a factor in forcing Pan American into bankruptcy.
Even with a hedging program in place, flaws in the strategy can lead to significant losses.
A spike in oil prices last fall to the highest level since the Gulf War hit revenues at Burlington Northern Sante Fe Corp, said Pat Ottensmeyer, the company's vice president of finance.

"Last year we were not properly hedged, and in the last three to four months of 1996, the fact that we weren't properly hedged cost us $29 million (corrects from $100 million) in fuel costs," said Pat Ottensmeyer, Burlington's vice president of finance.
Fuel costs account for 12 percent of total operating expenses at Burlington, the number two railroad in the U.S.
Ottensmeyer explained how a change of even one cent per gallon in the price of heating oil translates into an $11 million shift on operating expenses, or about four cents per share.
Currently, Burlington Northern is roughly 60 percent hedged for the remainder of the year, 32 percent for 1998, and about five percent for 1999, he said.
But for one of the world's biggest gold producers, Newmont Mining Corp, hedging plays virtually no part in the company's operating stragtegy.

"It is hard to see where hedging versus non-hedging has had a significant impact on shareholder value," Newmont Chief Financial Office Wayne Murdy said. "We are a low-cost producer, so we can afford to live with volatility."

That philosophy is unlikely to change in light of Newmont's recent takeover of Sante Fe Pacific Gold Corp, Murdy said. Sante Fe is hedged on virtually 100 percent of its production through mid-1998, equivalent to some 1.5 million ounces of gold, he said.
Newmont has yet to decide whether those positions would be closed or allowed to roll out through next year, Murdy said.
